title: Trapped Pieces
subtitle: A piece with no safe square is already lost.
goals: Punish greedy raids by taking away every escape square
Count a piece's flight squares before it grabs material
Cut your losses when your own piece is caught

steps.say: You don't always win a piece by attacking it — sometimes you win it by taking away every square it could run to. Black has just snatched the b2 pawn, and the queen looks safe: nothing attacks her twice. Count her escape squares instead. That's the trapped-piece question, and it decides the game right here.

steps.prompt: Black grabbed the b2 pawn. Punish the raid — trap the queen!
hints: Don't chase her: fence her in. Which white move attacks the queen AND removes her escape along the b-file?
Rb1! The rook hits her while the c1 bishop covers b2 — every square she can reach loses her.

line.say: The cage closes. Count her options: Qa3 and Qxc2 drop her to a minor piece, Qxc1+ gives queen for bishop, and Qxa2 walks into Ra1. There is no square on the board where she survives — one quiet rook move won a queen.

rejections.say: It attacks the queen — and she simply steps to a3, c3 or takes on c2. Chasing a queen usually just improves her. The winning idea is to remove every square at once: Rb1!

You captured her — but that was never possible for free: Black is not obliged to leave her there. The rook move keeps the attack AND the cage; here the bishop's job is to guard b2, not to trade itself.

steps.wrongSay: Stop thinking 'attack the queen' and start thinking 'which squares can she reach?'
steps.successSay: A trapped piece is worth more than any tactic: the opponent must simply hand it over.

steps.prompt: Now play the other side. Your queen is trapped — find the escape that costs the LEAST.
hints: She cannot be saved. When a piece is lost, the goal changes: get the most material for it.
Qxc1+! Taking the bishop with check means you lose queen for bishop plus a pawn instead of queen for nothing.

line.say: The right surrender. Queen for a bishop and a pawn still loses material — but 'lost piece' does not mean 'give it away'. Grab whatever it can reach on the way down, and prefer doing it with check.

rejections.say: Rb3! and the queen is rounded up for nothing at all — you handed over nine points and got zero. If a piece must die, it should take something with it.
Ra1! traps her again on a2 with no compensation. The c1 bishop was the only material within reach — take THAT one, with check.

steps.wrongSay: The queen is lost either way. Which escape square at least captures something valuable?
steps.successSay: Cutting losses is a skill. A doomed piece should always eat on the way out.

steps.prompt: Rewind one move: your queen eyes b2 and the pawn looks free. Knowing what you now know — what should you play?
hints: Before grabbing a wing pawn with the queen, count her escape squares from that square. Here she'd have almost none.
Develop instead. Any healthy developing move is worth far more than the b2 pawn.

line.say: Correct — a developing move, and the b2 pawn stays exactly where it is: poisoned. Masters call b2 and b7 'poisoned pawns' precisely because the queen who takes them so often never comes home.
Development instead of greed. Strong players do sometimes take on b2 — but only after counting every escape square, which is exactly the calculation most players skip.

rejections.say: And we are back to Rb1! trapping her. The pawn was bait: one pawn for a queen is the worst trade in chess. Count the escape squares BEFORE the raid, not after.

steps.wrongSay: The lesson of this whole exercise: don't send the queen where she has no exits. Play a normal move.
steps.successSay: Poisoned pawns punish greed. Now you'll count flight squares before every raid — yours and theirs.
